#4183. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#4182. Pikmin 4's Switch 2 Edition Has A User Score Of Just 1.8 On Metacritic

Nintendo added a new game to its growing library of Switch 2 Editions on November 12 via Pikmin 4, adding new features and attempting to add value to the paid upgrade by introducing a new mode based on the base game’s popular Dandori Academy. However, the user reviews are in, and fans of the series don’t believe the upgraded game offers good value for money.

Pikmin 4’s Switch 2 Edition scored an 83 on Metacritic with reviewers. Not had at all, and just a few points shy of the 87 its base game scored. The user reviews tell a different story. The upgraded version of the game currently has a user score of just 1.8, making it the worst-rated entry in the series by some distance.

Metacritic scores out of ten too, not five, so even worse than you might have initially thought.

Pikmin is a series that has served Nintendo well, scoring highly with both critics and players. In fact, until now, every numbered entry has a user score of at least 8.1. Pikmin 4 actually has one of the highest, with an 8.9. The limited additions to its Dandori Academy edition upgrade, however, have clearly left its fans feeling burned, and unlike red Pikmin, they aren’t immune to fire.

The user reviews for the Switch 2 Edition are a mix of the paid upgrade not being worth the asking price overall, and a focus on the Dandori Academy, the new version’s flagship feature, using too much content from the base game rather than adding anything truly new.

“Why spend 10 bucks for a slower game and rehashed levels?” one 0/10 user review reads. It also compares Pikmin 4’s new edition to the deluxe version of Pikmin 3 that launched on Nintendo Switch, which added a lot more new content to the game.

“The Dandori Academy has reused content, half of the maps so far are taken directly from the base game, and the other half share the same exact layout,” a 2/10 review reads. Complaints that the upgraded game now runs significantly more slowly seem to be a common complaint too. “This ‘upgrade’ of Pikmin 4 somehow manages to make the game run significantly worse, with standard load times going from six seconds to 30+ seconds,” another review claims.

This isn’t the first time Nintendo has come under fire for its paid Switch 2 Editions of games originally released on the Switch. Mario Wonder, Mario Party Jamboree, and Kirby and the Forgotten Land all now have Switch 2 Editions that mean the games cost $80, or you have to pay extra for the additional content if you own the game on Switch.

The complaints that those other Switch 2 Editions haven’t offered enough new content have been there, but have been much more muted than the backlash being thrown Pikmin 4’s way. It’s unclear if the content in this situation is so minimal that it warrants additional blowback, or if this is a case of Switch 2 owners being fed up with the paid upgrades offering limited new content and finally deciding to try and send Nintendo a message.

Pikmin 4's Switch 2 Edition brings some welcome upgrades to the original game, but whether they're worth the cost depends on your love for Pikmin.

#4181. The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Easter Eggs That Did And Did Not Make It Into The 2026 Remake

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is a game full of Easter Eggs, secrets, and hidden mechanics (did you know if a butterfly lands on your Deku Stick, it summons a fairy?). Now in its second remake, not every secret has made its way forward through the previous iterations, but many have. Below you will learn about a few of the secrets that made the cut, and others that didn’t.

In the courtyard where Link first meets Zelda, there is arguably the most fourth-wall-breaking Easter Egg in the whole game. If you don’t rush to Zelda and instead pause and enter first-person to look around, you will see portraits of other Nintendo characters through the windows, like Mario and Yoshi. In the 3DS remake, the portraits are replaced by an image of a Mario stage.

For the 2026 remake, there are no references to other Nintendo characters. Instead, the tapestry you build over the course of the game is on display. Removing the reference to Nintendo characters outside of the Zelda universe is understandable, but it is a little odd that art representing the full adventure of the game – an adventure that has not yet concluded – is on the wall.

As stated above, the Nintendo character portraits are gone, but there is still a guard you can annoy. If you fire a Deku Seed into the left window, a guard will pop out, yell at you, and then throw a bomb at you. You can’t pick up the bomb. In fact, at this point in the game, you haven’t even seen a bomb.

The Hyrule Castle portrait references to Yoshi and Mario are gone (though Mario and Luigi are still kind of in the game in a way), but Bowser gets a pass for some reason. Both Malon and her dad, Talon, are still wearing Bowser pins on their clothes. And unlike the N64 game where the detail was a little vague, there is no mistaking it here.

Gossip Stones are all over Ocarina of Time and it takes a while to understand what they do. If you hit them with a sword, they tell you the time, and if you play Zelda’s Lullaby near them, they refill your magic. If you do the Happy Mask Salesman’s side quest, interacting with them while wearing the Mask of Truth offers little hints and details about the world. But then there are interactions that are just odd for no reason. Blowing up a bomb near a Gossip Stone still makes it take off like a rocket ship, and using the Megaton Hammer still flattens them for a moment like a Looney Tunes.

And speaking of playing Zelda’s Lullaby for inanimate objects, if you slash a sign to pieces with your sword and regret your words and deeds, you can play the iconic tune to make the signs reform and become readable again.

This detail was exclusive to the 3DS remake of Ocarina of Time, and surprising no one, it has been removed. Ocarina of Time launched in June 2011 and Nintendo released Skyward Sword about five months later in November. For… marketing purposes, I guess, Skyward Sword art could be found in Lonlon Ranch, the Bombchu Shop in Hyrule Castle Town, and the Gerudo Fortress. It was a fun Easter Egg to discover back in 2011, especially since Skyward Sword was still months away, but these days it’s a bit of an odd inclusion.

Though never explicit, the composer ghosts guarding the Sun’s Song (and Link’s first ReDead encounter) have always been assumed to be inspired by Mario and Luigi. They are brothers; Flat is short, squat, and red; Sharp is lanky and green. They still appear in Ocarina of Time this way, which isn't surprising, since they are important characters you must meet to get a very useful song. Fans have also speculated that Talon and Ingo are Mario and Luigi-inspired for similar reasons, but it’s worth noting that they are not brothers.

In the Spirit Temple there is a large statue of a woman and for reasons that have never been explained, Link could attach his hookshot to her breasts. It served no purpose. It didn’t help solve a puzzle. If anything, it was confusing. But we all tried it and there is no shame in admitting it! That was removed for the 3DS remake, and it remains removed in 2026.

This is a very subtle reference to Wind Waker/Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom and is potentially the only addition to the remake that looks toward the future of the Zelda franchise. Obviously, plenty of characters in Ocarina later appear in Majora’s Mask (another remake of that is hopefully being considered), but it would be inaccurate to call those intentional Easter Eggs.

However, in Kokiri Forest and in the neighboring Lost Woods, the magical debris floating in the air often resembles a Korok as it would later appear in the series. It makes sense, too, because the Koroks are meant to be what the Kokiri transformed into following The Great Flood.

For more on the Ocarina of Time remake, you can find our review here. You can also find our interview with the game's producers here.

#4180. The Switch 2 Pro Controller Can Make Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Even Better

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time hit Switch 2 today, and, as Kyle Hilliard pointed out in our review, it is pretty excellent. Along with its remarkable visual upgrade, the new Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time adds quality-of-life improvements and modernizes the control scheme. As part of that, Nintendo has added the ability to jump and sprint. While that works well to make the game feel new, I quickly realized it sometimes clashes with another new improvement: a free camera controlled by the right stick. Holding down the sprint button to get through areas as fast as possible can make it tricky to keep the camera where you want it, but thankfully, if you have the Switch 2 Pro Controller, there's an easy fix.

After hours of running around, I was awestruck by the level of detail and updates, but I found myself constantly fighting with the camera, or at the very least, needing to take a strange claw-style grip to be able to direct the camera with the right stick, while holding down the A button to sprint. If you're a casual Switch 2 player, you might not have even noticed the back buttons on the Pro Controller, or you just have no idea what they do. Those buttons can be remapped on a per-game basis and it's a simple process. Everyone has their own preferences, but, for example, for high-mobility shooters, I like remapping one of those to reload and one to jump. I've never felt the need to remap in a Zelda game, but after feeling the need to do so with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, I might do so going forward.

If you, like me, struggle to comfortably steer the new free camera while running through hallways, towns, dungeons, and, yes, Hyrule Field, you might want to consider remapping your controller. As you can see in the above image, the placement of Jump and Dash on the face buttons can make it difficult to simultaneously control the camera and sprint. This isn't typically a problem in most modern games, as clicking the right stick is often a toggle to sprint, but in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, you need to hold the button.

If you have the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller, copying one button's functionality to the buttons on the back of the controller is simple. All you need to do is hold the Home button on the Switch 2 Pro Controller for a moment until the Switch 2 system menu appears on the right side. Along with Power Options and any Bluetooth audio devices you have available, there is also the option to map GL and GR, the controller's back buttons on the left and right, respectively.

Navigate down the menu to the GL and GR, then select which one you'd like to map. It will ask you which button you want to assign to the one you selected. Everyone can choose whatever makes sense in their own head, but mapping A (Roll and Dash) to GL and X (Jump) to GR made the most sense to me. Now, while I'm using the Switch 2 Pro Controller, I can use my middle finger to hold the GL button to Dash around without removing my thumb from the camera-controlling right stick.

And the best part is that, since you're not removing the functionality of the A or X buttons, you can still use them when it makes sense. For example, A also controls actions like opening up a treasure chest or door, and in my head, that feels like a face-button action, whereas rolling and dashing feel right mapped to the back buttons. The only downside is that, since this functionality is new for Switch 2 Pro Controllers, it isn't available if you're using the Joy-Cons or a Switch 1 Pro Controller. Also, it can make switching over to handheld mode challenging, as you don't have access to the back buttons in that play style.

Even if you don't have the ability to take advantage of this tip, either because you don't own a Switch 2 Pro Controller or because you prefer playing in handheld mode, you should still absolutely play the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. To learn more about the experience and why it's a must-play, head to our review.

#4179. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4178. "The Series Was In Dire Straits" - Kit & Krysta Recall Zelda's Pre-BOTW Dark Times

While many of us can now look back on the Skyward Swords of the Zelda series with fondness, those who were in the trenches at the time might recall that things were starting to feel stagnant.

The later games of the 'traditional' Zelda formula were well received critically, but the tried-and-tested gameplay wasn't working wonders for their sales numbers, and they were struggling to bring in new fans in the process.

Cue the open-world series reinvention in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

With Ocarina of Time back in the public eye (perhaps the most typical 'Zelda' a Zelda game can get), there are some who are wondering why it has been so long since we've seen the traditional format. So, naturally, former Nintendo employees Kit & Krysta are on hand to remind us all just how dark things were getting before the invigorating shot of BOTW.

"There has been some revisionist history out there lately about how the Zelda team 'ripped these [traditional format games] away from us at the peak of their popularity'," Kit Ellis said on the latest episode of the duo's podcast before setting the record straight.

"The series was in, like, dire straits," Krysta Yang added, "it was selling like nothing". Kit recalls going to focus groups and receiving feedback like, "the fanbase is dwindling; this is not bringing in new players; the interest is getting smaller".

With the huge success of Zelda today, it's easy to forget that such a time ever existed — particularly for those who weren't all that deep on the series at the time.

"It was depressing," Krysta adds, "it was like, we are losing this."

Of course, Breath of the Wild was so immensely popular and so very unlike anything we had seen from the series before that it gave Zelda the interest boost it so desperately needed. It's interesting to see how well-received the return of the classic format has been with OoT, so perhaps we'll see something slightly more traditional make an appearance in the next mainline game.

The dream scenario would be Nintendo leaving room for both formats to develop, but it's far too early to know what the team is cooking up for the next mainline entry. Until then, we have the pinnacle of the open-world structure and the very best of the traditional at our fingertips on Switch 2, so we're more than happy to wait and see what comes next.

Skyward Sword was also put into a weird position, I feel.

It required WiiMotion+ controls, and while they did work fine for me personally, for a lot of people it was really janky. And the failed tech demo of the game on stage where wireless interference made it almost impossible for them to show off gameplay really really soured a lot of gaming journalists and had a lot of people going in with a negative expectation. I remember article after article talking about how bad it would be. IIRC this was the last time Nintendo did their game announcements live - it's all been prerecorded Directs ever since!

Like I said, I feel it was largely fine. But it also meant the game couldn't be played as easily sitting down, and also meant that if you got the game without already owning a Wii Motion+ controller, you had to either get a new controller, or the adapter. (or get the game with the bundled controller)

The other aspect is that it was one of Nintendo's last (or was it THE last) games for the Wii - the push was being made for moving to the WiiU and the game didn't see any kind of upgrade for the WiiU other than it running through backwards compatibility. But there was no upscaled version or high res version or anything, so it looked like a Wii game on the new 1080p console.

That and the WiiU itself was a flop, and that didn't help either.

So I feel Skyward Sword just got super unlucky. And yes, it was rather linear compared to even Twilight Princess. But the story was really good but I wonder how much of it was the classic formula, or rather that it got mired in sometimes wonky controls, the pre-soured expectations, and being at the end of the Wii's life and not really getting a second chance until the Switch re-release. And even the re-release has it's issues - then Joy-con motion controls are not as reliably precise as the the Wii Motion+ controls and the pro controllers really show the game was not designed for classic controls at all.

@JohnnyMind I think you’ve hit the nail on the head with the sales data. Gaming as a whole was starting to recede in the late Wii era and we all knew the WiiU was a bomb. It was such a different landscape for gaming too.

That era’s “mainstream gaming” and today’s are very different. Gaming was still very much a niche hobby of sorts back then. A popular niche hobby, but still niche nonetheless. We were in the beginning of the live service transformation of the industry where most gamers wanted CoD or Halo and open world games were taking over and Nintendo, by contrast, was still delivering traditional style games.

I can totally see why Nintendo might’ve been nervous about what to do and how to adapt to how the market had shifted.

We forget too that, for all the success of the Wii and the DS, Nintendo hadn’t had the consistent domination they’re enjoying today, as the GameCube trailed far behind the competition. The Wii resuscitated them briefly for the casual market and most “serious gamers” were associating with PlayStation and Xbox at the time too.

The brilliance of their pivot with the Switch, BotW catering to the more “serious” gamers, embracing the indie market, and Mario Odyssey being a defiant and confident celebration of all things Nintendo is certainly a lesson for how to regain a crown.

"These two former Nintendo employees know absolutely nothing about Nintendo! I, the consumer, know the truth!" - A lot of you guys for some reason.

In June 2011, Ocarina 3D came out and sold pretty well. The it had given the 3DS another boom in units sold, but it didn’t last the whole Summer, resulting in a dramatic price drop for the system a couple months in, to make it cheaper than even the price which the DSi launched at.

But were certainly articles at the time about how Skyward Sword selling 3 million copies after the holidays was not satisfying enough. Both Donkey Kong Country Returns and Super Mario Galaxy 2 sold more than twice that amount. In the 2011 holiday season, Mario Kart Wii and New Super Mario Bros. Wii sold more, despite releasing in 2008 and 2011 respectively.

There was still certainly more hype and excitement than most games on the market. The big thing it was competing up against however was Skyrim, that just had universal praise and a virality like no other game at that time.

But, it was also a pretty late Wii game. Nintendo focused their efforts onto 3DS, which had made Skyward Sword a bit of a 2011 straggler. In that year, both Xbox and Playstation gained ground as incredible games were releasing then, alongside some more advanced motion-sensing technology to draw noise. The Wii was older news and had Skyward Sword released in 2010, like it was originally supposed to, I think you get a much different conversation about the popularity of that game. But, this sort of competition of Zelda getting slightly snubbed happens regularly too. Baldur’s Gate 3 narrowly sold more than Tears of the Kingdom, and snatched more awards too.

Regardless, in the 2013 Wii U Direct, Nintendo made it a point to say that the the next Zelda title after Skyward Sword would have its linear structure entirely challenged and go back to basics.

Before we even knew Breath of the Wild’s title, story, or aesthetic, Nintendo wanted to tell us that the structure would change and make it their selling point. You really only make that remark when you sense from your fans that they are ready for a change.

So, I do think that was because the series was viewed at as something very conservative in its approach and Nintendo caught on to that. The formula of a Zelda game was well understood and Skyward Sword did little to change that. Comparatively, A Link Between Worlds was looked at as something with a middleground between fresh and historied, being the sequel to the the game that would establish the “Zelda formula.” I don’t think it was in “dire straights,” to the extent that it was threatened as not being one of Nintendo’s most important franchises, but it was considered to be predicatable in its approach, and maybe even a little tired.

Skyward Sword was released in late 2011 when, as much as I love the console, the Wii was largely irrelevant. Twilight Princess was only 4 years old at that point and was a big hit as a launch title (TP is arguably the most ‘typical Zelda’ title there is, as it was designed to placate the backlash to the toon style of Windwaker and is very much a spiritual sequel to OOT and the Spaceworld 2000 demo we all expected would be the GameCube’s Zelda). It’s a bit disingenuous to suggest Skyward Sword sold badly due to being a ‘typical Zelda’ when really it was because most Wiis were probably gathering dust by then.

The Wii U we all know was a disaster, so again, blaming the low sales of Wind Waker HD and Twilight Princess HD on their typicality is not really accurate. BOTW was a Wii U title until (wisely) it was reserved for a launch game for Switch and a swan song for us Wii U owners. Had it not been a Switch game then there is no way it would have been the juggernaut that it turned out to be, with an install base of only 13 million Wii U owners.

A Link Between Worlds, OOT 3D and Majora’s Mask 3D all were good sellers on 3DS in the time between Skyward Sword and BOTW. In fact, the least popular Zelda game, Triforce Heroes, was the most different of all games and the time and was pretty much a disaster!

I really hate when people blame the level design for Skyward Sword's commercial struggles. I saw a lot of the trend/demand dying for Zelda when I worked at gamestop. The series has its diehard fans, but it wasn’t pulling in new interest. The stories were considered too lighthearted/childish by many mainstream consumers. They wanted adventure that was gritty, often bloody and less magical. Also less talkative (a complaint I will never understand about RPGS or adventure games) JRPGs were also hitting a downward tilt/over saturation and some of that is still a thing. People eat up soulsbore games for their bleak, difficult worlds and while the lore is dense…the player has to look for it (and half of that is inferred). While kids wanted shooters and ballers.

Nintendo tried to keep the formula fresh with control schemes and art styles but they weren’t seeing consistent returns. The Zelda cycle is/was a real thing as you’d watch a Zelda game get rave reviews but not the sales numbers to match or later become a misunderstood classic (WW,MM,SS,PH). BOTW changed that by essentially going back to Zelda’s roots. Here’s a big arse map, gather stuff to beat Gannon, good luck. The first Zelda game let you tackle the first 8 dungeons for the most part however you wanted (how hard that was or how many times you died was a different story) BOTW brought that back (and was less strict even as you don’t have to do the main story really to beat ganon). BOTW was also a launch/gen straddle game. I do think there is a natural surge in potential consumers as many fans are now middle aged and introduced their kids to the franchise.

I’m just glad Nintendo is stubborn about certain franchises. Which I suspect is more due to the producers in charge that believe in the franchise than anything. Nintendo has employees that either spent their lives working on these franchises or grew up with them. So it is still a product but there is almost a heritage aspect to it that many companies don’t have.

#4177. A Documentary About BioWare's Final Years Is Coming Next Year

A documentary is on the way, titled Massive Effect: The BioWare Story, will track the studio from its creation to its last two years. According to IGN, the documentary is produced by Shane Fennessey and Adam Scorgie and is being made for Canada‘s Super Channel and will release some time next year. BioWare was based in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada.

Geoff Keighley shared a few additional details about the upcoming documentary and confirmed his involvement as an interviewee.

Next year, the story of BioWare will be told in MASSIVE EFFECT: THE BIOWARE STORY, a new documentary that chronicles the history of the company and its sad closure by Electronic Arts. I was honored to be interviewed for it earlier this year. https://t.co/928LPZWK7H

— Geoff Keighley (@geoffkeighley) November 5, 2026

Late last month, news broke that EA was shuttering BioWare, the studio behind Mass Effect, Dragon Age, and more. Following the news, a work-in-progress teaser trailer leaked sharing what the team had been working on. Ea reportedly closed BioWare in favor of pursuing more Star Wars projects, which you can read about more here.

For Game Informer's own documentary of sorts, you can read our expansive oral history on the studio which covers its inception up to about 2016.

#4176. Award-Winning Composer And Musician Jon Batiste Talks Ocarina Of Time's Music And Why 'Guile's Theme' Goes With Everything

Jon Batiste has collaborated with the likes of Alicia Keys, Lenny Kravitz, Prince, Stevie Wonder, Willie Nelson, and many more. He performed the national anthem at Super Bowl LIX. He's headed up the musical efforts of The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. He's taken home more awards than we can realistically list in this article (including eight Grammys, as well as an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, and a Golden Globe). But as I sit down with Batiste for a brief conversation about video game music, his energy transcends the Zoom call.

Before I can even ask a question, Batiste begins singing to greet me, then nerds out about my NBA Jam and Street Fighter II cabinets. He begins humming the menu music from NBA Jam and reminiscing about all the quarters he pumped into his local Street Fighter cabinet. The Louisiana native and Juilliard School alum has been an ardent gaming enthusiast for nearly three decades, with compositions from games like Sonic the Hedgehog and Final Fantasy VII inspiring his earliest musical endeavors. Spend enough time watching video game music performances on social media, and you'll likely soon find videos of Batiste sitting with famed Final Fantasy composer Nobuo Uematsu, or of Batiste performing gaming music.

With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time delivering some of the most iconic music of all time (and Batiste famously loving the music), it makes sense that Nintendo would bring him out to New York to serve as a special guest at the launch event for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. I sat down with Batiste for a few minutes to chat about his love of video game music, his history with Nintendo, and why "Guile's Theme" from Street Fighter II just goes so well with everything.

Ocarina of Time is easily one of the most important video games ever made, and one of the things that makes it so special is the music. What about Ocarina of Time sticks out to you sonically?First off, if you want to get super inside baseball, technical music nerdery, which I love to do, in the compositions, there's a way that major chords and minor chords in... no sevenths, just root, third, fifth. They alternate, and it creates this magic that is, like, it's wistful, and it's simple. It feels ancient, and it feels like it's the music that is going on in your mind as you're generating thoughts and your imagination is churning. And the major chords are happening just after the minors in this contrary motion that's happening, so it feels like the music is going like this: It's going up – major, minor – like [sings the main Legend of Zelda theme song].

So, it's expanding and contracting, which is a musical allegory for the expansion and the openness of the world that Link is in. It's like [Koji Kondo] figured out how to capture the essence of the gameplay, but also the essence of magic and simplicity, which I think is really what makes... that's the music's power! So, you could listen to the music in the game, and you could also listen to it apart from the game and experience that magic.

Are there any tracks in Ocarina of Time that stand out to you as the most musically sophisticated or compositionally impressive?Oh man. Well, I think of it as a suite, so that's what makes it actually... there's nothing that's more or less complex, but the thought to figure out how to make all of the themes be interrelated yet singular. "Song of Storms" is, like, for me, that's a personal favorite. That's why I like to play it. I like to play a lot of the themes. That's how I grew up! I would play the game, and then, I would go to an instrument. Once we played for hours on Nintendo, we'd go and play Nintendo on piano! It was like a trade-off there, you know? I've been doing this since I was about 11 years old.

Taking it back to that 11-year-old Jon, talk to me a little bit about your history in general.Okay, so my history with Nintendo goes back to the NES. Christmas morning. Duck Hunt. You remember that? Maybe the first game I ever played. No, the first game I ever played was Donkey Kong, and then Duck Hunt, and then Super Mario Bros. Staples! We're talking about the early '90s. We had a room where I would go – it was my domain – and we had this blue shag carpet, and I would sit back there, and I would basically disappear into the carpet playing Nintendo for hours and hours.

And my mind is kind of... my mind can become a spiral; it can become a tornado. And I realized even then that going into this world of the game, even if I didn't win – it's not about winning or losing – it helps to organize the spiral of my mind and give me ideas and inspiration. So then, I started to get into Street Fighter II when I started to play more communally with my sister and my cousins. Yoko Shimomura, who I also had the pleasure of meeting and collaborating with, she composed incredible themes for each character, and that's when I really started to get a true love for fighting games.

And then, we would play so many of the Street Fighter franchise. We would play a lot of Final Fight. There were so many things... there was Double Dragon, then we got Mega Man... all these different series. Mega Man X is [an] all-time favorite. And then, here comes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and that sort of expands the canon while also blending all of the elements: score, combat, the sort of linear quality of, like, a Donkey Kong or Super Mario World, and expanding the world in that way, expanding the canon in that way. Mind-blowing! So,  that sort of solidified my palate in terms of my favorite type of game.

You mentioned Street Fighter II. There's a meme about "Guile's Theme" and how it goes with everything. What about that composition makes it so it has the ability to enhance whatever video you pair it with?Wow! So, it has momentum in a way that is extremely [sings the melody of "Guile's Theme"] ... It draws you in, which is what you want [with] anything that you're starting when you're commencing a journey or watching something. You want it to draw you in, and that kind of pulls you in as that call and response. But it's an immediate announcement with the brass, and then the bass call and response. So, it's automatically giving you this feeling that something's happening, and I've got to pay attention to it! So that's the first step right there. And the tempo is really... it's a great tempo! It almost has the feeling of the great themes from, like, an '80s protagonist that's in a fighting movie. I think that was kind of the archetype. Yoko was probably drawing from that archetype, right? The action-hero archetype.

#4175. Our first look at Diablo 4's Warlock and the game's next season arrive in today's livestream - watch it here

Diablo 4's latest Developer Update is nearly upon us, and it's one plenty of the game's fans and players have been looking forward to.

Diablo 4’s next, long-awaited Developer Update finally airs today. This meaty livestream was first announced nearly a month ago, when Blizzard initially revealed that the game’s next class is the Warlock.

The Warlock’s initial unveiling, however, was incredibly brief, showing no gameplay. It also didn't explain how the class is going to fit within the existing roster. This all changes today.

Blizzard is bringing back its Developer Update livestream programme, which is the more structured, information-dense series of developer showcases. The focus of this one, of course, is going to mainly be on the Warlock class.

The Warlock is one of two classes coming to Diablo 4 with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion. The first, the Paladin, is already available in the game for anyone who pre-orders the expansion. The Warlock will instead arrive alongside the expansion on April 28.

The Developer Update will also include a first look at the game’s next season (Season 12), currently set for March 10. This mini season will only last until the expansion’s release, so it’s going to be interesting to see what it brings to the game.

You’ll be able to watch the showcase live at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT on Diablo 4’s official YouTube, Twitch, and Twitter channels. We’ve embedded the YouTube and Twitch players below for your convenience.

Among the topics the Developer Update will cover are the Killstreaks system, as well as Bloodstained items. As always, you can also expect a Q&A segment at the end of the show, and I imagine there’s going to be a few about the Warlock.

#4174. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – November 6, 2026

This week and weekend is all about the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, one of the few games I feel deserves the title of masterpiece. And the remake is really well done! I got every heart piece, every Gold Skulltala, the Goron Sword, and the biggest pouch for every one of my items over the course of the review... but I am contemplating jumping right back in for another go.

We also revealed our next cover and in case you missed the announcement it is... pause for effect... Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis! It's an awesome cover that celebrates the history of Lara Croft, and along with a cover story on the game, we also have a big retrospective on the series. I highly recommend subscribing to get your issue if you haven't already.

But it wasn't all just Zelda and Tomb Raider this week. Below you will find a list of weekend play recommendations, but before that... some of our biggest stories of the week.

We have been writing a lot about The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time remake this week because it is one of 2026's most exciting games, and it's real good. The remake is not particularly surprising. It mostly sticks to the trajectory of the original game, but there is a reason it is considered one of the best games of all time. It also looks and plays amazing.

You can read the full review here (or watch the video above), but we also have a big interview with the game's producers (one of whom worked on the original Ocarina of Time, and one who directed Breath of the Wild among many other Zelda games), some details about the Easter Eggs that did and did not make it into the remake, and a very handy tip for the game if you happen to be playing with a Switch 2 Pro controller.

World of Warcraft: Forever is out now and it’s a great time to jump into the revamped and expanded version of a project that changed online games forever back in 2004. A thousand new quests, multiple new zones, countless revamps, and an impressively stunning visual overhaul make it the perfect time to jump in for anyone who’s ever been curious to explore Azeroth.

2022's Escape Academy was a sneaky little puzzle game that surprised me and its sequel released this week. Taking place in a school obsessed with puzzles, you play as a student who must make their way through a series of escape rooms. The puzzles are clever, and the setting is charming, but the secret weapon is the local, split-screen co-op. Solving puzzles together is fun especially when one player needs to look at one section of a room to help dictate a solution on the other side of the room. My wife and I both love video games, but rarely play co-op games together just because of our disparate, individual tastes. But Escape Room is one we enjoyed together and we're so far enjoying the sequel. My only complaint so far is... I wish it ran a little better.

While we collectively use the term here for the sake of familiarity, I’m always a bit hesitant in my own mind to label a game under the wide banner of “Metroidvania.” In part, that’s because I think the two referenced games (Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night) are actually more different than they might appear at first glance. Gloomsoft’s recent release, Moadra, recognizes that distinction, crafting a game that draws heavy inspiration from the specific tradition of Super Metroid, even while presenting an intriguing and atmospheric fiction that is great fun to discover. In movement, actions, and exploration, Moadra feels remarkably similar to  the best of the 2D Metroid games. A scanning tool also leans into the Metroid inspirations, revealing details about the weird alien world you’re navigating. If you’ve been hungry for a game that scratches that particular itch of sci-fi gear/ability-gated exploration, I think you’ll find a lot to love in this game.

I get the Marvel fatigue we've all been experiencing. There are a lot of games and a lot of movies and a lot of TV shows and many are good, but lately most feel like homework. For those reasons, you'd be forgiven for dismissing the 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy game, but I promise you it is good. For one, it is standalone. It does not directly tie to any specific Marvel media. No homework necessary. And for two, it's just a really good game with an affecting story and a unique take on the characters that most of us met for the first time in the movies. And, for the BioWare fans out there mourning the loss of Mass Effect, this game has some Mass Effect energy. It's available on Switch 2 this week and I happily recommend it, especially if you missed it five years ago.

This exclusively two-player board game features a fun mix of activities. You act as both a dungeon architect, and an adventurer delving into said dungeons. Each player creates their own version of a challenging dungeon filled with traps, monsters, and treasures.

But you’re also forced to take on the dangers of your opponent’s crafted dungeon, to see who manages to come out on top. If you have fond memories of the hidden-info nature of old games like Battleship, but you want some greater strategic depth and fantasy flavor thrown in, this one is a great pick.

#4173. GTA 5 And Red Dead Redemption 2 Are Leaving PS Plus

Even though tens of millions of us will be playing GTA 6 later this week, Rockstar wants to make sure the player count is as high as possible. That even means sacrificing player counts in their other games, as GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 are leaving PS Plus.

The two most recent Rockstar games have been available to play through PS Plus Extra for the past few months. The games are routinely added to Plus and then removed, with their latest arrivals - particularly when it comes to GTA 5 - Rockstar’s final push to get as many people playing its games before GTA 6 arrives.

Every game coming to Essential, Extra, and Premium and the dates you'll be able to play them for free.

GTA 5 and Red Dead 2 will be removed from Extra on November 17 at midnight, which means today, November 16, is your last chance to play them on Plus. Not only a chance to jump in and play them for a few hours if you don’t already own them, but also your last chance to play if Extra is how you’ve been playing them up until now.

That’s because, unlike Essential games which remain in your library and playable as long as you have an active subscription, Extra games come and go. When a game is removed from Extra, you can no longer play that game unless you pay for it, even if you have it installed on your console.

Games are removed from Extra’s library around halfway through every month, but GTA 5 and Red Dead 2 being a part of this batch is unquestionably a tactical move on Rockstar’s part. While there will undoubtedly be people who play GTA 5 for years to come - it has sold more than 200 million copies and has an online element that GTA 6 won’t have at launch - Rockstar will still want to do every little thing possible to ensure as many people as possible are playing GTA 6 from November 19.

There is an argument to be made here that the better approach would be to leave GTA 5 on PS Plus in an attempt to attract more people to GTA 6. It’s a tactic sports series, which release a new game every year, have been using for a while now. EA Sports FC, for example, will see its latest game added to PS Plus around nine months after release. That gets more people playing and, in theory, convinces new and lapsed fans to buy the new entry right away three months later because they don’t want to wait for it to be added to Plus a year later.

Rockstar is taking a different approach, and if you want to play a GTA after today, you’re going to have to pay for it. Odds are that GTA is going to be GTA 6, although it will be fascinating to watch sales numbers over the coming months to see if there’s a similar pattern to the way Mario Kart has sold. Despite the release of Mario Kart World, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe continues to sell incredibly well. Perhaps we will see the same thing happen to GTA 5 and GTA 6.

Time to pre-order GTA 6. Here's everything you need to know before securing your copy ahead of release.

#4172. 10 Games That Have Creative Punishments for Cheating

Shane is a Contributor for DualShockers writing guides and other materials. He has a degree in Game Design and Criticism.

It’ll come as no surprise to any gamer that pretty much every game has a way to cheat, whether it's approved by the developers or otherwise. Over the years there have been some pretty creative and hilarious ways that developers have dealt with cheaters in all kinds of games from FPS games to the cozy ones.

While a lot of the punishments for cheating in more recent years are typical things like warnings or outright bans, there are some that take a more creative approach. Whether it’s a fun way to kill the player or an incredibly punishing turn of events for dark deeds, it’s always funny to see that happen.

This list consists of many games from all sorts of genres and ages, but they all have some interesting and hilarious punishments for what they perceive as cheating. It may not always be altering game files and could just be something players are able to abuse in game.

Way back in 1996 Crusader: No Regret came out following in the footsteps of its predecessor Crusader: No Remorse. The isometric gameplay combined with some great weapons and destructive environments made a very engaging combination.

The only problem was if you played the previous game and attempted to use any cheats from the last game Crusader: No Regret would have something to say about it. Players would be greeted with a message and teleported into a room with eight copies of the final boss.

Heretic was created using the DOOM engine, but things were a bit mixed up and instead of the traditional DOOM world this one was steeped in fantasy elements. Everything revolved around the fantasy element as players could use magical weapons like the Elven Wand, and Phoenix Rod.

Unfortunately for players who were well educated in the ways of DOOM, the developers had a surprise for anyone hoping to use DOOM cheats. Inserting the cheat for God Mode would instantly kill players, and the all weapons cheat would instead reduce you to using just a wooden staff.

With the recent remaster of Ocarina of Time there’s a lot of great details in the Legend of Zelda series coming to light. Some are just fun little tidbits or small things, but in Link’s Awakening the dev team decided to make things a little harder for anyone doing nefarious things with Link.

Link can steal some items from a shopkeeper by distracting him and then grabbing the items to take outside. Not only does doing this ruin Link’s reputation earning him the mark of thief by any other NPCs, that shopkeeper will also kill Link to settle the debt.

Activision is drawing a line in the sand against third party lobby shopping apps, threatening bans outright.

Traditional MMOs typically don’t play too well with cheaters, resulting in all kinds of punishments, but one MMO really stands out, EVE Online. This old school MMORPG is all about space battles and exploration in its entirely player driven world.

During a GM Week event there were public executions of cheaters who had been caught and the team opened up the destruction of these ships to any players who wanted to join. This turned it into an incredible spectacle that many will not soon forget.

The Sims series is probably one of the most prolific gaming franchises on the planet, being enjoyed by a huge demographic of people. Even in these cute games people try to cheat and The Sims devs were not going to let that slide even on the DS.

If you attempted to use the internal system clock to skip time forward the game would notice and spawn an alien invasion that would cause a lot of problems. They become a persistent problem in the game and could require players to restart the game.

To combat rampant cheating, BULKHEAD implements ping locks to keep certain regions out of main servers.

CD Projekt Red are known for their storytelling and incredible game design, but they don’t just stop being amazing there. While the devs respect when players are able to find something they hadn’t accounted for they didn’t stop them from doing it, they just got a bit creative.

When The Witcher 3 originally came out there was an exploit that would let you kill cows in the starter area indefinitely giving you crazy amounts of money. To fix that they simply spawned a giant late game monster, a Chort, that would likely kill players as a punishment.

There’s nothing quite like finding out a classic game has punishments for attempted cheating, and Pokemon Ruby and Sapphire is no exception. Despite being a game for mostly young people they weren’t going to stand by and let someone cheat in their game.

Pokemon, of course, has a way to mess with players who were able to manipulate game code although it's a bit different from others on the list. Instead of anything dangerous the game would spawn a Bad Egg in a box that cannot be moved creating an issue with inventory for the rest of the game.

Cheat codes in games have been around for longer than most gamers, so a lot of early games allowed players to put them in. Now just like some other games, they want to encourage you to still play the regular way and have to get a bit more creative about punishments.

Banjo-Kazooie took this to an extreme and offered players the ability to put in forbidden codes doing all kinds of silly things. If you put in too many Gruntilda will threaten to erase your save file, making this a very dangerous gamble if you aren’t careful.

A config exploit is helping losers disconnect from Marvel Rivals matches without penalties.

Edmund can’t ever do something in half measures and Mewgenics is more than proof of that in almost every aspect. The game took a lot of things to extremes and dealing with cheaters is no exception.

If you tried to save-scum, quitting out of something quickly to reload a previous save, the game would know and you’d meet Steven. The first time you do this in a run he gives you a warning, but if you continue to do it you’ll no longer have control of the game and Steven will make all the choices.

Not many games have the sense of humor that The Stanley Parable has and this, of course, has to extend beyond the metaness of the game. This hilarious narrative game wants you to focus on the order of events and not have you screw that all up.

If a player attempts to use console cheats the game takes notice and sends them to the Serious Room where the narrator has some choice words for them. Continuing to do it only makes the punishment longer and more ridiculous, much like everything in the game.

From giant heads to low gravity, these are the PS2 Games That Had the Most Ridiculous Cheat Codes — and Why Players Still Miss Them.

#4171. Review: CRKD Ult Pro Controller For Switch 1 & 2 - A Decent Pad Let Down By Awful Shoulder & Bumper Buttons

CRKD is the latest accessory manufacturer to produce a premium alternative to Nintendo’s own Pro Controller on Switch 2, but it’s one that needs a lot of refinement if it’s to become a legitimate competitor.

Priced at $69.99 / €79.99 / £64.99, the Ult Pro sits below the Pro Controller and roughly at par with Gulikit’s excellent TT line, price-wise. It comes feature-packed with TMR (Tunnel Magnetoresistance) analogue sticks, Hall Effect triggers, four back buttons, two extra bumper inputs, four profile modes, adjustable rumble, a charging stand, and more.

The analogue sticks feel good, featuring a more convex shape that you don’t often see these days. There’s a thin ridge near the edge of the grip which helps keep you aware of where your thumbs are sitting. It’s also worth mentioning that the grips can be removed for replacement designs, but these are sold separately – it would have been nice if at least one alternative were included in the box as standard. Otherwise, the TMR technology should keep stick-drift at bay.

The default D-pad design (again, you can swap it out if you want) is circular with a raised cross representing the four cardinal directions. I like this a lot: it feels quiet yet retains accuracy during gameplay, and I found it reliable for platformers like Super Mario World and action games like Contra.

The ABXY buttons unfortunately aren’t mechanical with a satisfying click, but they do the job well enough. Like the analogue sticks, they’re slightly convex in design and are spaced at just the right distance to allow easy, intuitive access to all of them. I also like the colours; CRKD avoided the exact same colour scheme as both the SNES and Xbox 360 pads, but it’s got the same vibe (you can also opt for an all-black controller, if you wish).

The shoulder and bumper buttons, sadly, let the side down. You can adjust the shoulder button travel distance, opting between a short, clicky input or a full, smooth trigger input. To be clear, the Switch 2 doesn’t support analogue triggers for anything except the Nintendo Switch Online GameCube pad, so your choice here is purely down to personal preference.

While the full-motion trigger feels pretty good, the clicky, tactile option is horrible. Rather than offering a satisfying click, they instead feel weak and spongy, almost as if the slightest bit of force will snap (or ‘CRK’, amirite) whatever mechanism is inside to produce the clicky response. I hated this, and CRKD should address it promptly for any future revisions.

As for the bumper inputs, the additional ‘L2’ and ‘R2’ inputs are far too close to the main ‘L1’ and ‘R1’ buttons on either side. So essentially, when resting your index finger across the bumpers, you’re covering both the standard button and the extra input, making it far too easy to accidentally press the wrong button. CRKD would have been wise to space these further apart and make the main bumpers larger (8BitDo’s Pro 3 is a good reference point), or just remove the extra inputs entirely.

Speaking of extra inputs, the four additional buttons on the rear are perfectly fine – I’ve got no major issues with these, and they’ll no doubt prove useful for anyone looking to gain the upper hand in Modern Warfare 4 (or perhaps even sprint while moving the camera in Ocarina of Time). The only downside is that they produce quite a loud click when pressed, though I think this is down to the plastic used for the exterior casing – it feels a tad cheap for the price.

You can map any input to the additional buttons — the four on the back and the two on top — by using the ‘P’ (Program) button underneath the D-pad. You also have four profiles if you want to swap between configurations. CRKD neglected to include decent instructions with the product, and the QR code for an online manual led me to a dead page, but it does at least have a video on YouTube if you need help remapping buttons and setting up profiles.

With the function buttons (i.e. Start, Select, Capture), CRKD bizarrely opted for two rocking inputs. With the left one, for example, you push it up for Select and down for Capture. It’s so weird – it works, but it’s weird. There’s no dedicated ‘C’ button; instead, there's an integrated macro to navigate to the Chat app if you push down on the right rocker.

You can connect the Ult Pro to your console via three different methods. Bluetooth is standard and works exactly how you’d expect: just hold down the large, black button until it flashes blue to enter pairing mode. You also have a USB dongle stored inside the charging dock, so plug this into your Switch 2 dock and you can pair that way instead. Finally, you can simply connect it via a USB-A to USB-C cable. The difference between these is, for me at least, not noticeable, but if you’re someone who’s particularly sensitive to lag, you might have a clear preference here.

Oh, and there’s no wake-up support for Switch 2. Sorry.

Finally, the Ult Pro lasts for around 15 hours on a single charge, and if you use the included charging dock, you’ll likely never need to worry about it dying on you. The dock design is simple and looks neat next to the TV when charging. You can also replace the rechargeable battery in the controller itself if need be, or simply use a pair of AA batteries.

There’s a lot to like about the Ult Pro, including its TMR sticks, the D-pad, the charging dock, and the lovely coloured ABXY inputs. Unfortunately, CRKD really dropped the ball with the shoulder and bumper buttons – I hate them, and they really ruin the whole thing for me.

With no wake-up support and a fairly cheap-feeling exterior case, this isn’t quite the Pro Controller competitor I was hoping for, but with some tweaks and refinements, I think the company could be onto something. Do I actually like those rocking function buttons, though? Honestly, I’m still not sure.

The sample used in this review was provided by CRKD.
